To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the test sets that are used for digital chips are not adequate for detecting all the defects that are present in the chips.

the single-stuck-at fault model is not a good predictor of defect coverage, and that test set size reduction techniques that are based on preserving single stuck fault coverage do not preserve defect coverage.

(1) the defect coverage of a chip can be significantly improved by using test patterns that are specifically designed for the chip and (2) the test escapes of the test sets can be reduced by using test sets that are specifically designed to reduce the number of test patterns.

the development of a methodology for the design and test of VLSI circuits.

the characterization of the defects and the development of techniques to reduce the test set size.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single technique that is best for all applications and that each designer must choose the appropriate technique for his particular situation

the use of single-stuck-failure models is not a good strategy for test set generation and that the test set generation techniques that are compatible with the single-stuck models are not the most effective techniques for test generation.
, in general, there is a significant penalty in test quality when using test sets that have been compressed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a single stuck fault model to represent defects is not adequate.
there are no magic bullets.
the use of structural test sets for digital logic is a very effective technique for reducing the test set size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
test escapes occur for many different types of faults.
the test escapes can be reduced by using test sets that are larger than the minimum fault coverage sets.
, in order to achieve a high quality test set, it is necessary to retain the defect coverage.
